title: Reading Literature: Meaning and the Reader
text:
Literary criticism has long been divided between those who regard a text as a self-contained object and those who insist that it can only be understood in relation to its historical moment. The New Critics of the mid-twentieth century championed close reading, arguing that meaning resides in the words on the page rather than in the author's intentions. Their opponents, drawing on Marxist and psychoanalytic traditions, contended that every interpretation is shaped by the ideology and assumptions of its reader.

Reader-response theorists went a step further, locating meaning in the encounter between text and reader rather than in either alone. Wolfgang Iser, for instance, argued that texts contain deliberate gaps, or 'blanks,' that the reader must fill in through imagination. Such theories unsettled the notion of a single, correct reading, though critics still debate whether this openness amounts to genuine plurality or merely to a more sophisticated form of subjectivity.

questions.text: According to the passage, what did the New Critics emphasize?
options: The historical background of the author's life
The meaning contained in the words on the page
The psychological state of the reader

questions.text: What did Wolfgang Iser argue that texts contain?
options: Deliberate gaps the reader must fill

questions.text: What can be inferred about the opponents of the New Critics?
options: They believed the reader's own ideas influence how a text is understood
They rejected the study of literature altogether
They considered the author's intentions the only valid source of meaning
They thought texts had no connection to any historical context

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about the debate over reader-response theory?
options: It has been settled in favour of a single correct reading
Critics agree that openness always produces true plurality
It remains unresolved whether its openness is genuine plurality
Critics have abandoned the idea that the reader plays any role

paragraph_translations: A crítica literária há muito se divide entre os que veem o texto como um objeto autossuficiente e os que insistem que ele só pode ser compreendido em relação ao seu momento histórico. Os Novos Críticos da metade do século XX defendiam a leitura minuciosa, argumentando que o significado reside nas palavras da página, e não nas intenções do autor. Seus opositores, apoiados nas tradições marxista e psicanalítica, sustentavam que toda interpretação é moldada pela ideologia e pelas suposições de quem lê.

Os teóricos da recepção foram além, situando o significado no encontro entre texto e leitor, e não em nenhum dos dois isoladamente. Wolfgang Iser, por exemplo, argumentou que os textos contêm lacunas deliberadas, ou 'espaços em branco', que o leitor deve preencher com a imaginação. Tais teorias abalaram a noção de uma leitura única e correta, embora os críticos ainda debatam se essa abertura representa uma pluralidade genuína ou apenas uma forma mais sofisticada de subjetividade.
